entries.content:
This is Dolores Jeanette Harrison, who was the smartest girl at Cleveland High School in Cleveland, Alabama. She probably would have been the smartest girl at your high school also, but being the daughter of a failing farmer in Blount County, Alabama isn’t a recipe for success, so I can’t point you to an online biography of her — though I will say that she worked full-time, with two breaks to bear children, from age 15 to age 80. She was a bookkeeper and accountant; always a math whiz … at least until recently.

Her name is unusual. She was the eighth child in her family and by then her mother was tired of coming up with names, so she delegated the task to her older daughters. They named their new sister after two favorite actresses, Dolores Del Río and Jeanette MacDonald.

Dolores married young. I don’t know much about that marriage except that it didn’t last long. She moved to Birmingham and got a job in a bank, where one of her co-workers introduced her to a nephew, Carl Jacobs. Carl and Dolores married in 1955; they had two children, one of whom is me.

After my father’s death she continued to live in their home in rural northern Alabama, a dozen or so miles, across Blount Mountain and Sand Mountain, from where she grew up. A family friend bought her a puppy named Ansel, who became her best friend and major comfort. She was terribly lonely after my father’s death, and tended to mope. My sister once suggested that maybe she could try to move on, at least to some extent: “It’s been fifteen years since he died.” “Fifteen long years,” Mama quietly replied.

In the spring of this year she took a bad fall in her bedroom, and it soon became obvious that she could no longer live in her home; it was also evident that Ansel, now quite elderly too, was failing badly. In short: she lost everything that gave her life order and comfort at once, and since then has been rapidly declining.

About a month ago my wife Teri spent an afternoon with Mama and, during their talk, encouraged her to trust in the love and mercy of Jesus. This Mama said she did, which is a comfort to me, especially since she and my father were only intermittent churchgoers at best, and never spoke one word to me about their beliefs or lack thereof.

(I must take that back: My father once said to me that his time in Japan and China in the years following the Second World War, when he was in the U.S. Navy, made him ask why we believed that our religion was truer than theirs. Only because it’s ours, he thought. Thus was completed my religious education at home.)

Mama has dementia of some variety, probably Alzheimer’s, though it’s impossible to know for sure. It has been developing for some time, but her recent loss of coherence has been precipitous and dramatic. When I saw her ten days ago she seemed aware that I was someone she knew, but did not recognize me. She spoke of my brother — I don’t have a brother — and later that day told her nurse that she has two daughters (she has but one). Of greater concern and pain to me is the utter transformation of her personality: she has always been calm and quiet — I have quite literally never heard her so much as raise her voice — but now she is chatteringly manic. She also is often paranoid: she told me that there are nurses in her care center who try to drown her. (They try to bathe her.)

Before I saw her I had been grieving that I’m hundreds of miles away; now that doesn’t bother me so much — what would be the point of being closer? — but I am grieving in a different way.

But there is one more thing to say. The day before I arrived she was relatively serene and coherent, and had an affectionate talk with my sister. My mother and my sister have never gotten along, and open affection has never been part of my mother’s emotional repertoire. But on that day she held my sister’s hand and told her how much she loved her. She said that she has had a good life.

My sister asked her whether she remembered being married. She thought about that for a moment and then said “Yes.”

“Do you remember who you married?”

“Well … who am I?”

“You’re Dolores.”

“Oh! Then I married Carl! I loved him very, very much. And he loved me.”

entries.content:
Many of you know how much I love The Walter Martin Radio Hour. I’ve been listening (and subscribing) to it almost since the beginning, and it’s been a constant source of pleasure and indeed joy for me. His enthusiasm is certainly contagious, but the greatest value here is the depth of his musical knowledge and the sheer number of tracks he has hipped me to that I would not have known about otherwise. (Here I think especially of his recent three-hour playlist of Jamaican pop music from the Fifties to the Seventies.) But his constant ragging on Paul McCartney in this remarkably long Beatles season has annoyed me. I must mouth off.

My first annoyance came when Walter did his series on Paul: he said almost nothing about Paul’s work after 1978 or so, and for his Paul-post-Beatles playlist picked outtakes, oddities, and stuff Linda did. (Walter likes Linda.) Macca has produced a buttload of mediocre music, to be sure, but there are also some really good things — for instance Flowers in the Dirt (1989), and especially the fantastic demos of those songs that he did with Elvis Costello. There are a number of terrific pop songs on Flaming Pie (1997) and Chaos and Creation in the Backyard (2005).

Why didn’t Walter mention any of this stuff? My assumption is that he has never heard it and dislikes Paul intensely enough that he was unwilling to give it a listen. But what that means is that his Paul-post-Beatles playlist yields a profoundly distorted view of what Paul has accomplished. I’m not saying that Walter needed to have a serious encounter with the McCartney discography; but if he didn’t want to, he should have just said that he didn’t want to and therefore would not make a playlist. What he did instead is a just a gratuitous insult to Paul, it seems to me.

Now, do I regularly listen to Paul’s post-Beatles music? With the exception of those demos with Elvis, no. But then, I don’t listen to John Lennon’s post-Beatles music either. I don’t think either man is one-tenth as interesting alone as the two were with each other and the other Beatles. But if you’re gonna treat George’s post-Beatles career with respect (which Walter did) and you’re gonna treat John’s post-Beatles career with respect (which I certainly expect Walter to do when the time comes), then Paul deserves the same treatment.

But Walter can’t get over his distaste. In the currently ongoing John Lennon series, he interprets everything John does in the best possible light and everything Paul does in the worst possible light. If John wants to experiment in the studio and do weird things with mics and introduce delays and promote other sort of imaginative engineering — and he was constantly pressing the EMI engineers in such ways — then wow, the dude is so cool, he’s so creative. Buhen Paul wants to do it, he may well be attempting to “sabotage” John’s music.

The facts are: Each of them could sometimes care about the success of the group and could sometimes be selfish. Each could have a great insight at one moment and come up with a stupid idea the next. The stupid ideas weren’t usually malicious or manipulative or controlling, they were just stupid. (Everyone in that studio from 1965 on was coming up with stuff, all the time. Paul has talked over the years about telling the engineers “Just try it, if it doesn’t work we can erase it and do something else. Just try it.” Often they did erase it after all … but not always.) Neither John nor Paul was a saint or a faultless genius, and picking suspiciously at everything Paul did while celebrating everything John did is just partisan cheerleading. It’s not true to the actual situation.

N.B. Ian Leslie does the best job of capturing the real dynamic.

One of the other things Walter complains about is Paul’s “hot-dogging,” as he calls it, on the bass in some songs. Also on backing vocals. Now, before we get to that, we need to distinguish this point from what might be thought a related one. Paul, who has a plausible claim to being a better guitarist than George (see the P.S. below) and was obviously a far superior guitarist to John, didn’t get that many chances to play guitar for the Beatles. Especially in the first half of the Beatles’ career, he was largely confined to the bass at a time when pop-music bass playing was expected to be very simple and placed very low in the mix. So Paul was always fighting with the EMI engineers, who were afraid that if you increased the volume of the bass then, when the vinyl record was played, the needle of a phonograph could jump out of its groove. For safety’s sake they always kept the bass levels low, and you can barely hear Paul’s playing on many of those early songs (unless you’re listening to a modern remaster).

Do you think any of the other Beatles would have been happy with having their contribution to the song virtually inaudible? (Even Ringo wouldn’t have liked it.) So Paul was always getting the engineers to listen to songs recorded in the USA, especially Motown songs, and saying, “Listen to the bass here. If they can do it, why can’t we?” And as far as I can tell, all the other Beatles backed Paul on this point. I don’t think there’s a controversy about this; I don’t think even Walter would believe that Paul was out of line in wanting his bass to be more prominent in the mix.

But distinct from the question of how audible his instrument was is the question of what, exactly, he was playing. Among rock and pop bassists Paul was a virtuoso, and so he naturally wanted to explore the possibilities of the instrument, wanted to see what it and he could do. For Walter, this is a bad thing … when Paul does it. (Some other artist trying to explore the possibilities of his or her instrument would probably be awesome. But with Paul, it’s hot-dogging.)

Now: Does Paul overdo it sometimes? Goodness gracious yes. For instance, I think — and George Harrison strongly agrees with me here — that his playing is way too busy on “Something.” But the song that precedes “Something” on Abbey Road is “Come Together,” which also has an elaborate bass line — and it’s brilliant. Almost universally revered, though probably Walter dislikes it. But a great musician trying to extend the possibilities of his for-too-long-marginalized instrument isn’t going to nail it every time; and it’s not an unforgivable crime for him to go overboard occasionally. Heck, Paul and Ringo both go nuts on “Rain” and it’s the best rhythm track in the whole Beatles catalogue.

One reason for Paul’s over-elaboration, I think, involves the way the Beatles recorded their songs in the latter stages of their career. Once the band, working with George Martin and the engineers, got a basic track established — drums and rhythm guitar usually — then the various Beatles would add any further contributions later, on their own. Often Paul’s bass would be the last element recorded: he sat in a studio by himself and listened to the rest of the song on headphones as he worked out his part. It’s the kind of situation that invites too-muchness, a problem that Paul was aware of, as can be seen by his enthusiasm for getting the band to record as a band again: thus the Get Back sessions. But being aware of the problem was not the same as overcoming it. The temptation to overdo was always right in his face.

Paul’s leadership of the band in the studio is another thing that Walter can’t really forgive him for, but here’s the thing: as John, in the mid-Sixties, got more and more drug-addled, he wrote fewer and fewer songs. (The ones he produced tended to be bangers, though.) It’s vital to understand that if Paul had not stepped up and taken a more dominant role — if he had not become a kind of organizer and the cheerleader for the group as well as its primary songwriter — the Beatles might very well have fallen apart as early as 1965. And even if they had managed to hold together in some form, they could not possibly have produced anything remotely like Rubber Soul, Revolver, and Sgt. Pepper. It was Paul’s leadership that made those records possible, even if John wrote some — most, I would say — of the coolest music for them.

Is that what anybody would want? A world in which Paul stays politely in the background and just plays his one-two-three-four (I-V-vi-IV) walking basslines, doesn’t write too many songs, and waits for John to come out of his most recent drug coma? It sure as hell isn’t what I would want. Paul could be over-elaborate in his playing, and he certainly could be bossy and OCD — Ian MacDonald is right to say that the most correct brief answer to the question of why the Beatles broke up is: “Maxwell’s Silver Hammer” — but cast your mind back to 1965 and 1966 and look at the results.

I have mouthed off. (All that said, you should absolutely subscribe to the Walter Martin Radio Hour. It’s amazing.)

P.S. Re: Paul and George as guitarists, I think Paul was technically superior in that he could play sequences of notes that George couldn’t manage, at least not at Paul’s desired tempo. But George played many beautiful riffs and solos that Paul could have played if he had thought of them; but he never would have thought of them. George had a feel for the kind of sparely elegant melodic or harmonic line that Paul would have disdained; as a guitarist, George simply had better taste.

entries.title: undermining Babylon System
entries.summary: I’d suggest listening to this song while reading this post — it’ll help you understand the point of my use of italics. Most of my work is about literature and the arts, and I like it that way. I plan to keep it that way. In fact, I plan to go even further in that […]
entries.content:
I’d suggest listening to this song while reading this post — it’ll help you understand the point of my use of italics.

Most of my work is about literature and the arts, and I like it that way. I plan to keep it that way. In fact, I plan to go even further in that direction than I have. But I also have a long history here on this blog of thinking out loud about political and social issues, and I have been, over the course of the last fifteen years or so, elaborating an argument that I would like to summarize right now, with links to the key posts. I’ve written some interlocking series that collectively constitute the extended form of this argument, but here I will try to summarize my case as concisely and pointedly as I can.

What most Christians — on the theological right, the theological left, and in the middle — fail to understand is the fundamental distinction between the city of God and the city of man. We (by which I mean “those total losers among my fellow Christians, and certainly not me”) are always trying to transform the city of man into the city of God, or else pretend that the city of man can be tuned, as it were, to divine purposes. These tendencies keep us enmeshed in the workings of the city of man, and cause us to neglect our citizenship in the city of God.

This, by the way, is not an argument against voting. It’s not an argument against political activity. It’s an argument against confusing the city of God and the city of man. You can work for the good of the city of man without making the mistake of believing that you are a citizen of it.

The biblical image of the city of man, and therefore the permanently relevant symbolization of this, is: Babylon. We live in Babylon. We do not live in a Christian America, we do not live in a fundamentally Judeo-Christian framework. We live in Babylon. And Babylon is owned and operated by transnational powers, which can be conceptualized in one of two ways. You can say that Babylon is run by a kind of collaboration between (in theory) democratically elected governments and multinational corporations. Or you can say that the city of man, Babylon, is run by what the Apostle Paul calls the Principalities and Powers. Both of these descriptions are correct as far as they go, but the former is more useful when it is seen as but a practical outworking of the latter.

In this sense, the briefest and best name for the regime under which we live was given to us by Bob Marley: it’s Babylon system. It is a far-reaching, multi-tentacled network of forces that enlists us in its own projects. So when we’re fighting it out on social media — whether Christians are fighting against non-Christians, or Christians of the left are fighting Christians of the right — what we’re all doing is treading the wine press. We are doing the work of Babylon system.

It’s slightly comical that the people who most intensely despise one another are performing the same labor for the same boss. What left and right are really trying to do is get management to take their side in some particular dispute, but in so doing they ensure that management remains management. Babylon system remains sovereign, building church and university … deceiving the people continually. The Prince of this world remains the Prince of this world. He will promise you victory over your enemies and he may even deliver it: but when you sell yourself to him in order to gain such a triumph, there’s no option for manumission.

So what is required in order to offer meaningful resistance is to stop treading the wine press — to decentralize, to disaggregate, to localize, to refuse and disobey. This is why I recommend anarchistic practices. James Scott, in Two Cheers for Anarchism, talks about strategies of resistance that begin with simple non-cooperation:

Quiet, unassuming, quotidian insubordination, because it usually flies below the archival radar, waves no banners, has no officeholders, writes no manifestos, and has no permanent organization, escapes notice. And that’s just what the practitioners of these forms of subaltern politics have in mind: to escape notice. You could say that, historically, the goal of peasants and subaltern classes has been to stay out of the archives.

You can start with non-cooperation. Your employer may insist that you have a presence on LinkedIn, let’s say — so have one, but don’t post. And when you do post, do in the spirit that Wendell Berry has recommended: Every day do something that does not compute.

We don’t have to retreat into the literal wilderness, but we do need to retreat into local and material lives that are not at the command of Babylon system. When you buy a paperback book and scrawl your thoughts in the margins rather than scroll through your social media feed, or when you buy a CD or a vinyl record rather than subscribe to a music service and listen to whatever the algorithm feeds you, you’re doing what will not compute — quite literally. Ditto when you trade herbs and vegetables with your neighbors, or even when you pay for the coffee of the person behind you in line. (You thereby make yourself more legible to the Powers in order to make them less so.) You can repair rather than buy new, and that goes for ideas as well as manufactured products. You can practice handmind.

These are very small refusals, tiny ways to act in the city of man as a citizen of the City of God. But very small refusals make a path for bigger ones, and in the very long run can make Babylon system a falling empire. It’s important to remember, as James Scott says, that “A great deal of the symbolic work of official power is precisely to obscure the confusion, disorder, spontaneity, error, and improvisation of political power as it is in fact exercised, beneath a billiard-ball-smooth surface of order, deliberation, rationality, and control.” The Principalities and Powers are not as mighty as they contrive to appear; and resistance to them is never futile.

Oh, and one more thing: about all this, Tell the children the truth.
